beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson two. {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}}, {{NADH|N A D H}} and the stepwise harvest. [[balloon]]Pop a balloon full of hydrogen near a flame, and all its energy leaves in one bang, as heat and light. [[stairs]]Now picture the same drop taken one stair at a time. Nothing bangs, and each step can be put to work. [[map]]Here is our map of cellular respiration. [[lit]]Today we light up the arrows that carry electrons across the top, and see why a cell takes the stairs.
beats.redox: [[eq]]Start with the overall equation. One glucose and six oxygens make six carbon dioxides and six waters, and energy is released. [[ox]]Glucose loses electrons, and loses hydrogen with them. It is oxidized. [[red]]Oxygen gains electrons, and gains hydrogen, and becomes water. It is reduced. [[move]]So respiration is a long move of electrons, travelling with hydrogen atoms, from the fuel all the way to oxygen. [[drop]]And on the way, they fall in energy. That fall is what the cell harvests.
beats.dehydro: [[fuel]]But electrons do not jump from glucose to oxygen directly. Glucose is taken apart in a series of steps, and at many of them, the first helper is an enzyme called a dehydrogenase. [[take]]The dehydrogenase takes two hydrogens from the fuel molecule. That means two protons and two electrons. [[nad]]It hands the two electrons, and one proton, to a molecule called {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}}. [[free]]The other proton is simply released into the surrounding solution. [[fuel2]]The fuel loses electrons, so it is oxidized. {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} gains electrons, so it is reduced. That makes {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} the oxidizing agent. The slide draws a generic fuel molecule, not glucose, because glucose goes through several of these steps. We will meet them in lessons four and five.
beats.pair: [[ring]]{{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} is a coenzyme, a helper molecule that carries electrons. Its working part is a ring, called nicotinamide. [[plus]]In the oxidized form, the ring carries a positive charge. [[gain]]Add two electrons and one proton, and the charge is cancelled, and an extra hydrogen sits on the ring. [[nadh]]Now it is {{NADH|N A D H}}, the reduced form. [[eqn]]The slide writes this as {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} plus two H in brackets, gives {{NADH|N A D H}} plus a proton. The two H in brackets just means two hydrogen atoms, two protons and two electrons. [[back]]And the change runs both ways. Give the electrons away, and {{NADH|N A D H}} is oxidized back to {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}}.
beats.q1: Quick check. What does a dehydrogenase do to its fuel?
beats.store: [[bus]]Think of {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} as an empty shuttle bus. At the fuel, it picks up two electrons, and it is now {{NADH|N A D H}}. [[full]]The full bus is stored energy. Those electrons are still high in energy, and the cell can tap that energy to make A T P. [[ride]]So the bus rides to the electron transport chain, and unloads its electrons there. [[return]]Then it is {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}} again, and goes back for more. [[few]]The cell holds only a small supply of these molecules, so they must be reused over and over. If the buses stopped coming back, the fuel could not be oxidized at all.
beats.steps: [[one]]Now compare two ways of making water. In the first, hydrogen and half an oxygen react in one step. [[boom]]The energy drops all at once and leaves as heat and light, an explosion. [[many]]Respiration makes the same water, from two protons, two electrons and half an oxygen. But [[chain]]the electrons from {{NADH|N A D H}} go down a chain of carriers. [[stair]]Each carrier hands them to a slightly lower one, so the free energy falls in small steps, like a staircase. [[atp]]At each stage, a part of the energy is captured to make A T P, and the rest leaves as heat. [[o2]]At the bottom waits oxygen. It takes the electrons, and the protons, and forms water. Oxygen is the final acceptor, and its pull is what keeps electrons coming down. The picture draws three A T P bursts and four complexes, but those are only drawings. We count the A T P properly in lesson seven.
beats.q2: Quick check. What happens at the end of the chain?
beats.example: [[a]]Let's put it side by side. Two ways to release the same energy. [[b]]Burn the hydrogen. One step, one big drop, all of it as heat and light, nothing the cell could use. [[c]]Now the cell's way. Many steps, many small drops, and some energy caught each time. [[d]]Same start. Same finish, water. The difference is how the drop is divided, and that is the whole idea of this lesson.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Glucose is oxidized and oxygen is reduced. Electrons travel with hydrogen, and fall in energy. [[s2]]A dehydrogenase passes two electrons and a proton to {{NAD⁺|N A D plus}}, making {{NADH|N A D H}}, a carrier of stored energy. [[s3]]{{NADH|N A D H}} delivers electrons to the chain, where they go down in small steps to oxygen, and water forms. [[end]]Now try the practice.
